newsitem.title: LEBANON: Japan's hopes of quick Red Army extraditions fade.
newsitem.headline: Japan's hopes of quick Red Army extraditions fade.

text.p: A Japanese envoy indicated on Monday that Tokyo no longer expected Lebanon to deport detained Red Army suspects immediately but still hoped for an extradition agreement after Lebanese justice runs its course in the case.
Hiroshi Hirabayashi, chief foreign policy adviser to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, spoke with reporters after talks with Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.
Hirabayashi handed Hariri a letter from Hashimoto on the issue, Lebanese government sources said.

"The Japanese prime minister said in his letter that if the suspects are proved to be Red Army members they should be dealt with on the basis of the crimes they committed against the international community," a government source said.
Some of the suspects are believed to have been involved in a Red Army attack in 1972 at Tel Aviv's Lod airport in which 24 people were killed and 100 wounded.
However, Hirabayashi said he expected the suspects to be dealt with first by Lebanon.

"We hope that after finishing the Lebanese judicial process, the Lebanese authorities will proceed in an appropriate manner to accommodate the Japanese authorities' concerns about the issue," he said.
This appeared a change in Tokyo's position. Officials there had previously said they wanted Lebanon to deport the suspects and were ready to send an aircraft to Beirut immediately to fly them home.
In a comment apparently linked with Hirabayashi's statement, an official Lebanese source told Reuters:
"The (extradition) issue is now in the freezer. It is not probable that Lebanon will hand over any suspects. They will be prosecuted in Lebanon for crimes committed in the country."
Lebanon and Japan do not have an extradition agreement.

Hirabayashi arrived in Beirut on Sunday to join efforts to resolve the case which has caused confusion between the two countries since Hashimoto said on February 18 that Lebanese officials had told him they had arrested six Japanese suspected members of the group in Lebanon's eastern Bekaa Valley.
Hirabayashi said after his talks with Hariri: "We are very optimistic that we will reach a satisfactory solution to the matter.
"We discussed how to proceed on the issue of the Japanese nationals detained here including some Japanese nationals who are believed to belong to the Japanese Red Army."
Hirabayashi later met Foreign Minister Faris Bouez and Prosecutor General Adnan Addoum. He was due to meet President Elias Hrawi before leaving for Syria on Tuesday.
He said he might raise the Red Army issue with Syrian officials. Syria has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and is the country's main power broker.
Judicial sources in Beirut said on Friday Lebanese authorities had started interrogating nine or 10 detainees who were mostly Asians and included three Japanese.

"We have many elements which indicate that they (some of the detainees) may belong to the Japanese Red Army but to be able to say clearly you have to wait maybe 24 hours," Hirabayashi said after meeting Bouez.
Asked if the confusion had negatively affected ties between Japan and Lebanon, Hirabayashi said: "No, to the contrary. I am very optimistic".
